full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing. Are you doing the Air Transport Management?

Subject:	Air Transport Management, yes.

Interviewer:	We’re mainly looking at engineers. I’ve spoken to some people on your course that don’t really consider.

Subject:	It’s not really engineering, no.

Interviewer:	But we’re also talking people under the wider umbrella of engineering, so if at any time I refer to engineering and you don’t think it is engineering just say. The main thing that we’re looking at is male dominated professions anyway – that’s why we’ve included you in the study and what we’re doing is looking at women engineers from all different departments and asking them about how they decided to do engineering and about their experiences of their course so far and what they’re expecting and whether or not they’re going on placement, and at the end of it all we’re going to put together a guidance document, to give to the Engineering Council to hopefully improve the retention of women in engineering. Are you going on a work placement?

Subject:	Yes, I am yes.

Interviewer:	OK, I’ll start off asking you like a few background questions and about how you decided to choose this course and things like that. Did you do ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	I did yes.

Interviewer:	What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did Geography, French and then I did 2 ‘AS’ levels, which was maths and physics.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a Catholic school.

Interviewer:	Ok, was that a mixed school?

Subject:	It was, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, What do your parents do are either of them engineers or in the Air Transport Industry?

Subject:	No, my dad’s a – dad’s a – owns a restaurant and my mum’s a housewife.

Interviewer:	OK. When and why then do you think that you wanted or decided to study air transport management then?

Subject:	Erm, well initially I wanted to do business – but then, I’ve always liked air transport, so I thought well, I wanted to be an air hostess before but it’s sort of air related anyway, and engineering didn’t – I didn’t really look at engineering, I looked at air transport. Yeah, I’ve always liked air transport and that’s why I went into it.

Interviewer:	OK. Did you decide that you wanted to do that, before you chose you’re ‘A’ levels, or after?

Subject:	I think during my ‘A’ levels – I was looking through the UCAS thing and what courses were available, and then I saw air transport management at [this university]. My sister was studying here anyway, so I sort of knew the area a bit anyway. And there wasn’t any other courses, like that air transport management, and that’s why I applied for it.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have any other influences or any advice that helped you make your mind up – did you have any careers advice?

Subject:	No. (laughter) I just went for it. I liked the sound of it, and then I looked at the modules, and it looked alright.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think it is that really appeals to you then?

Subject:	What appeals?

Interviewer:	Appeals yes.

Subject:	Er, I think it just sounds really exciting when erm – erm I don’t really know. It sounds interesting, I guess. I mean every time I tell somebody that I’m studying this, they go ooh, wow, you know. What does that involve or what do you study in that? But then we study a bit of everything really, like finance and you know, a bit of logistics, economics, just everything really.

Interviewer:	Yes, so its very broad. OK, did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Erm, I did because I knew it would improve my chances of looking for a job afterwards. I knew it would be hard, but I didn’t know how difficult it is, till I got to go for the second year – I did research. Then I started to apply to companies and you know, the interviews were quite tough and I think quite a lot of people have given up already.

Interviewer:	Ok, I’ll talk a bit about that later on. When you decided to come and do an air transport course, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I didn’t. I didn’t actually think about it but then when I got here and we had a (?) there was like 10 girls in you know, the whole class, which was like different people. Like you – I think air transport is quite like a sort of male dominated area. Always, in the past some – you know – I mean women, and I mean I think the only job people think of is probably like an air hostess or you know.

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you that there weren’t many women?

Subject:	No not really, I don’t think so but I’ve heard they’re creating more opportunities for women. For example pilots – they always used to be men but now, apparently, there’s quite a lot of female pilots, and female captains as well. I think the industry is changing. I think in the future, I want to go into the air transport industry. I think it shouldn’t affect me too much.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged into the air transport industry?

Subject:	Erm, I’m not so sure about encouraging them in – well, it goes down to whether they want to go into the air transport industry but hmm, it would be nice. I mean like you talk about engineering – you see more women mm, I mean my sister studies engineering and it’s – there’s quite a lot of men and I think she’s the only female and then she applied for a placement and the companies wanted females – and I think one of the reasons that she was employed, well for a summer placement – one of the reasons was you know, because she was female and she had it really easy apparently in the interview stage so…

Interviewer:	So that’s like an advantage, do you think there are any disadvantages to being a woman?

Subject:	Probably when you’re actually working, there are people – when you graduate – erm, perhaps there aren’t enough females around, it’s all males and maybe you’d feel it’s quite intimidating or…

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good air transport manager?

Subject:	What characteristics? Er, hmm, I’m not really sure. I think – I don’t really know actually. Erm, well being an air transport manager obviously you’ve got to know a bit about the industry, you know then you not only have to – you have to know a bit about the airlines but you probably have to know a bit about the engines as well. I know it sounds a bit silly but we study engines as well, you need to know a bit of everything, so. You need to know the industry – you know, like what’s going to effect it? I don’t really know, it’s quite broad actually, it’s quite difficult – you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think because you’re there on the management course that you think they could have more sort of people skills than other people on engineering courses?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely – people skills are an advantage to go off because, you know, you come across quite a lot of people, like customers, passengers, you know, things like that. And yeah I think a lot of – well you need office skills as well, I think, it’s not all about meeting people, I think you spend quite a lot of time in the office as well. I mean I’ve looked at some jobs and they – most of them say they want a, someone with experience in – you know, they want an office environment.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK, do you think that any of the characteristics that make a good air transport manager, are more male or more female characteristics?

Subject:	Er, I don’t think you know that there’s male characteristics or female characteristics. I think at the moment when you look at erm through er the air industry – most of them are males but erm one of the managers or the head of a low cost airline is a female. I can’t remember who it is?

Interviewer:	Is it [company]?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it was, yeah. That’s kind of gone – it merged with Easy Jet, so but yeah, that was – she was female.

Interviewer:	Do you find that encouraging when you see like…?

Subject:	Oh definitely, yeah. Yeah, I think – well it’s hard enough getting to you know, the industry, because you look at some of the jobs and er I went for a job interview and it was only for like the check in thing and er there was quite a lot of competition. You get people with like there’s loads of you know, many years, in the industry, and quite a lot of different people and I was the only student. It was only like a part time job and I – it was really difficult. I didn’t get that. I don’t know – you know – I don’t think it was because I was a female, so you know, it was quite equal.

Interviewer:	OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, some parts it has. You know I have some parts are what I expected but other parts, which is the engines, weren’t actually what I thought I’d study and that – I’m not only interested in the engine part but then we had to study like car engines as well and I don’t know why – what – where that came from. I don’t see it being relevant to my course. And we did that last year. I mean last year the course was – all the modules were really varied and we did train, buses and cars, trams, things like that. It’s not just air transport, it’s the transport industry in general, so.

Interviewer:	OK, what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing about the course is well we don’t have that many lectures. We don’t have that much – but the worse thing is you get a lot of course work – yeah, I think that’s one of the bad things. I mean we have 4 coming up and I haven’t actually finished – started - any of them. I’ve been really busy during Easter, I had to go and find accommodation, because I’m going on placement, for next year.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased that you did choose this course or…?

Subject:	I am pleased that I did because apart from this course, I don’t know what else I’d do. So I think if it wasn’t for this course maybe I probably wouldn’t have gone to University. I know it sounds a bit extreme but I looked at all the courses and I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t want to do business, I didn’t want to do engineering, you know, sort of like mainly engineering like you know electronics or something like that.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	None?

Subject:	None.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	I think so, yes. It would be nice because men they’re all – erm you know there’s nothing wrong with them – what I’m going to say is that they’re quite sort of old, I think they’re about 50, 60 you know, and they’re all male.

Interviewer:	So you just have someone younger?

Subject:	Oh it doesn’t matter. I mean they do – they’re very good at what they’re doing but it would be nice if we had like females, you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Yes. There’s no difference, yes.

Interviewer:	Ok, that’s good have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	I have.

Interviewer:	Are they male?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you happy having a male personal tutor or would you like to have a female?

Subject:	It doesn’t really matter, yeah, because even though he’s my personal tutor, I mean, I don’t actually see him that much (OK). But he teaches 2 of my modules and er, so I see him when I have problems with it.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Erm, I wouldn’t say so much the biggest influence, you know. But erm, some of the lecturers are quite good and it makes you think oh you know, I want to be – try and go into the industry because they’ve been in the industry before, and he’s worked for years and he’s been teaching now and he’ll tell you like what sort of things have happened, and how it can be fun and exciting and it can sound very interesting.

Interviewer:	OK, have you’ve had to do much group work as part of your course?

Subject:	Erm, so far I think we’ve got – we’ve done 3 group work sort of projects.

Interviewer:	And how do you decide who you work with when you’re working in groups? Do you get put into groups or do you get to choose?

Subject:	Erm, we get put into groups.

Interviewer:	OK, and have you had to generally work with men or women or a mix of both?

Subject:	Erm, well it’s generally men because there’s like only 10 females in my class. At the moment, I’ve got a group project and its all males. It hasn’t been a problem.

Interviewer:	No? Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work then?

Subject:	I think so. I think females are more hard working, I don’t know, but that’s what I feel, ‘cos men can be a bit of a – not all of them but some people in my group the men, seem a bit laid back.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Yeah. I’ve got one now and I had one last year. I think it’s – you know when we don’t co-operate, it didn’t – doesn’t actually work out. I didn’t actually think it’d be this hard you know like a group – because you get some members of the group who don’t want to work and they don’t turn up at meetings. I mean I’ve only seen like one person in my group, there’s 5 people and there’s 1 that never turns up and I’ve only seen him twice, you know in the whole year probably. Erm, that can be a problem and we haven’t got anything sorted out yet.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are benefits to doing group work though?

Subject:	Er, there are benefits, it’s just erm the work is split and you probably does less, instead of like the whole thing yourself. You get to discuss er things with other members and they can come up with great ideas as well, so yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the skills that you learn in group work will help you when you go into the industry?

Subject:	I think it will but in the industry I think it will be a bit more hard working, yeah. I don’t think it would be how they are now.

Interviewer:	What skills do you think that you’ve learnt from the course that will help you when you’re on your placement?

Subject:	Erm, well probably – probably the group work part where you have – when you have different kinds of people and you have to learn to work with them. So that’s probably one. But erm apart from that, I think it’s just what I’ve learnt in the sort of modules and what I’ve studied and just my knowledge really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel like you’re ready to go on placement now?

Subject:	No, I keep thinking you know, what are they going to give me to do? And I’m really worried they might so, oh go and improve this bus network something. That I’m – yeah I’m really worried that I just might come across quite stupid, you know, I hope they won’t give me anything really hard – or I won’t understand it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you for going on placement?

Subject:	Er, I think they could probably talk a bit more about the industry itself and you know, what to expect. Because at the moment I don’t really know what to expect. I mean not only in the air industry, it’s also like the transport industry, in general because we do quite a lot of other types of – kinds of transport. But a lot of people from my course have done something with air, like you know I think I’m the only person who hasn’t. They’ve all either you know, been at like an RAF camp or something, during the summer, or have flown before, you know, like as a pilot or done something to do with air, and I’m probably the only person like who hasn’t and I don’t know a lot about the industry. So, I think they could probably tell us a bit more.

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to any students that have been on placement previously?

Subject:	No I haven’t. But – I mean we have been told a bit about you know what they do. Not a lot of people actually get placements at airports or airlines. They do logistic companies or erm you know, transport planning, that’s the main area.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you’re going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m going to [place].

Interviewer:	To the airport?

Subject:	No, it’s like a [company].

Interviewer:	I see why did you decide to go on placement? What attracted you to doing a placement?

Subject:	Erm, I think the main thing’s experience. I don’t have any at all, like we’ve said. Er, and the one year would be really good. It would be quite – quite a lot of experience I think. And I also think, well get away from studying for a year er because it’s quite – it’s quite hard actually where – I mean even though you get Easter and Christmas but then you work through, through those holiday periods anyway – you get so much course work and exams straight afterwards. It’s not really a holiday I don’t think, you know. I suppose that’s what I think. I want to get away for a while and earn a bit of money, you know.

Interviewer:	OK, what attracted you to the company that you have got your placement with?

Subject:	Erm, it’s like a public sector company. I think maybe that what attracted me and er it’s – they’re responsible for the [____] erm in [town] and around [town] and erm I don’t think – it sounded you know, quite a good company and I wanted to apply to it because I wanted….

Interviewer:	Did you apply to any other companies?

Subject:	I did. They were all transport planning based. So I mean it’s not like I didn’t want to go into airports or anything like that but there wasn’t anything available when I started applying. I mean there’s a few now like erm [name] airport but I’ve already got my placement so I didn’t apply to that one anyway.

Interviewer:	Did you look at anything like training opportunities or career prospects, anything like that?

Subject:	Well, they didn’t actually mention a lot about you know, future prospects and things like that, but training yeah. So they sort of discussed all the – discussed in interviews that the training you along the way and quite a lot of companies now put a lot of emphasis on training. Yeah, I think with my company they do that as well.

Interviewer:	OK, how involved were the university in helping you find a placement?

Subject:	Well they have a tutor who’s responsible, you know, for emailing about placements and he’s really good and you can approach him at any time. I mean I did, about my placement, because I’d been to two interviews, I failed them and then he talked me through. He talked me through them and I explained where I thought I’d gone wrong and he explained what I should have done and it does help. So he – they are quite good. I think they have – well they do have quite a lot of contacts as well and there’s quite a lot of placements coming through by email now, you know. But it’s a bit late now, when you’ve got to apply and we’ve all got placements and that’s it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s anything else that the university could do to help you?

Subject:	Er, I don’t really know. Like I said they could probably tell you what to expect and what you could be doing because erm they’ve done this for a few years now. You know, had feedback from previous placement students but we haven’t really been told much about it.

Interviewer:	OK, you’ve probably already hinted what you’re most worried about on the placement but what do you think will be the best and the worst things about being on placement?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing will probably be having a salary – probably. And er, probably getting away from studying for a little while. Erm, the worst thing will probably be having to work 39 hours a week. Erm, and er I’m not sure about how much work you’re gonna get because I think you do get like – projects given to you. And I’ve got a brother who’s erm doing placement at the moment, and he’s studying engineering. I heard that he said he’s got a lot of projects and things like that. After you finish one you get another one. After you’ve finished another one you get another one and I’m not sure whether it’s going to be like course work, where you get like a huge load - that’s probably the only thing I’m worried about but…

Interviewer:	Do you know yet what sort of work you will be doing on your placement?

Subject:	Erm, I’m not too sure, no but I just heard that I’ll be working with like other members of staff and I’ll be working in a group and that’s all I know.

Interviewer:	Is there anything you’d particularly like to do while you’re there, or wouldn’t like to do?

Subject:	I’d like to learn more about the transport industry because there’s quite a lot of jobs in transport planning because the Government wants to improve the transport network and so I’ll learn as much as possible and erm I think I’ll probably go into transport planning if I enjoy the year out.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Erm…

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll get treated differently?

Subject:	I think you do because I think you get treated as an employee, you know, because you get paid as well and er I think it’s a lot more different than er when you’re a student because there’s so many students, you know, and the lecturers can’t sort of focus on each of you individually. When you’re an employee there’s only so many, you k now, people and you get somebody who’s looking after you. That’s probably – probably quite good – what was the question, I think I’m going off the point.

Interviewer:	No, that’s fine. How do you think work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Oh yeah. I can’t remember what else.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Erm, hopefully I’ll finish the course and graduate. And er, hopefully I’ll go into transport planning – if I enjoy my year out next year then I will go into transport planning, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what about in say 10 years time, do you see yourself going into like managing people?

Subject:	Erm, I think its probably something that – yeah, I’ll probably you know look forward to doing, but even if I don’t go into transport planning, you know, after I’ve graduated or something, I think I will try the air industry and I was thinking the other day, I’d probably still want to be an air stewardess, or something still in the air related industry. That’s just where my interest is.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think is your ideal career then?

Subject:	Erm, probably working in the air industry. Erm, but my dream has always been like to be an air stewardess really. I think I’ll probably just do that – probably do that, you know for a few years and that’s well, what I end up doing.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve that?

Subject:	I don’t think so. Well, I will but it’s not like because it’s a male industry or anything. I mean I’d enjoy being an air hostess, there’s quite a lot of females and I’ve heard it is quite tough cos you get like er so many tests, so many rounds of you know, different kinds of tests. It will be difficult but not because er it’s a male industry…

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to work abroad then?

Subject:	Hmm, I would like to work abroad but I’m just worried about the language difficulty. But I think, yeah

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the career prospects are good in air transport or transport generally?

Subject:	I think so, yes, because erm well the air transport industry it’s increasing and it’s you know – a lot more people – well people are travelling by air now than 10 years ago. It’s more accessible to people’s low incomes, and it is expanding and there be more planning – the same in the transport industry – the planning and all that.

Interviewer:	What about once you get into the industry for like climbing the career ladder?

Subject:	Er, God, the career ladder. I think it will be very competitive and from what I’ve heard and my experiences of trying to get into the industry, and applying for jobs – I think it will be very tough.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	No, I think I’m quite happy with – you know – what I’ve done and you know.

Interviewer:	OK, if you had to describe the transport planning industry, erm what 5 words would you use?

Subject:	Erm, what 5 words? Erm, probably erm – transport – all the air transport or transport industry?

Interviewer:	Yeah – either or both.

Subject:	Erm, well probably expanding, competitive, exciting, interesting and erm I don’t know, I can’t think of 5 things, sorry.

Interviewer:	OK. Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Erm, I think it probably generally is but yeah, I think it is.

Interviewer:	Do you think that is just because of the numbers of men? 

Subject:	I think so yeah, because transport I think it’s always been sort of like a male thing. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	Erm, I think – well it’s because like back – probably about 100 years or so. Like flying was invented by men and I think it’s been controlled by men, ever since, in a way and Governments as well. That’s why probably it’s a male thing and I think males are generally more interested in planes – there’s not a lot of females around y’know that like to keep planes, or plane spotting, or whatever.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women?

Subject:	I think it will, yeah. Like for example pilots – there are more female pilots now, so yeah.

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think the fact that it is male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	Erm, not very much I don’t think but I don’t know yet you know until I actually graduate and apply for jobs – because the few companies that I – I’ve been to, they were more men than you know females – I could see. So it’s – maybe they’ll decide on that basis, I don’t know really, not until I’ve graduated and so…

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything thank you very much.

I mean every time I tell somebody that I’m studying this, they go ooh, wow, you know. What does that involve or what do you study in that? But then we study a bit of everything really, like finance and you know, a bit of logistics, economics, just everything really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, so its very broad. OK, did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I did because I knew it would improve my chances of looking for a job afterwards. I knew it would be hard, but I didn’t know how difficult it is, till I got to go for the second year – I did research. Then I started to apply to companies and you know, the interviews were quite tough and I think quite a lot of people have given up already.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, I’ll talk a bit about that later on. When you decided to come and do an air transport course, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn’t. I didn’t actually think about it but then when I got here and we had a (?) there was like 10 girls in you know, the whole class, which was like different people. Like you – I think air transport is quite like a sort of male dominated area. Always, in the past some – you know – I mean women, and I mean I think the only job people think of is probably like an air hostess or you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it ever bother you that there weren’t many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No not really, I don’t think so but I’ve heard they’re creating more opportunities for women. For example pilots – they always used to be men but now, apparently, there’s quite a lot of female pilots, and female captains as well. I think the industry is changing. I think in the future, I want to go into the air transport industry. I think it shouldn’t affect me too much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged into the air transport industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’m not so sure about encouraging them in – well, it goes down to whether they want to go into the air transport industry but hmm, it would be nice. I mean like you talk about engineering – you see more women mm, I mean my sister studies engineering and it’s – there’s quite a lot of men and I think she’s the only female and then she applied for a placement and the companies wanted females – and I think one of the reasons that she was employed, well for a summer placement – one of the reasons was you know, because she was female and she had it really easy apparently in the interview stage so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So that’s like an advantage, do you think there are any disadvantages to being a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably when you’re actually working, there are people – when you graduate – erm, perhaps there aren’t enough females around, it’s all males and maybe you’d feel it’s quite intimidating or…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good air transport manager?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What characteristics? Er, hmm, I’m not really sure. I think – I don’t really know actually. Erm, well being an air transport manager obviously you’ve got to know a bit about the industry, you know then you not only have to – you have to know a bit about the airlines but you probably have to know a bit about the engines as well. I know it sounds a bit silly but we study engines as well, you need to know a bit of everything, so. You need to know the industry – you know, like what’s going to effect it? I don’t really know, it’s quite broad actually, it’s quite difficult – you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think because you’re there on the management course that you think they could have more sort of people skills than other people on engineering courses?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely – people skills are an advantage to go off because, you know, you come across quite a lot of people, like customers, passengers, you know, things like that. And yeah I think a lot of – well you need office skills as well, I think, it’s not all about meeting people, I think you spend quite a lot of time in the office as well. I mean I’ve looked at some jobs and they – most of them say they want a, someone with experience in – you know, they want an office environment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, OK, do you think that any of the characteristics that make a good air transport manager, are more male or more female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t think you know that there’s male characteristics or female characteristics. I think at the moment when you look at erm through er the air industry – most of them are males but erm one of the managers or the head of a low cost airline is a female. I can’t remember who it is?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it [company]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it was, yeah. That’s kind of gone – it merged with Easy Jet, so but yeah, that was – she was female.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that encouraging when you see like…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh definitely, yeah. Yeah, I think – well it’s hard enough getting to you know, the industry, because you look at some of the jobs and er I went for a job interview and it was only for like the check in thing and er there was quite a lot of competition. You get people with like there’s loads of you know, many years, in the industry, and quite a lot of different people and I was the only student. It was only like a part time job and I – it was really difficult. I didn’t get that. I don’t know – you know – I don’t think it was because I was a female, so you know, it was quite equal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, some parts it has. You know I have some parts are what I expected but other parts, which is the engines, weren’t actually what I thought I’d study and that – I’m not only interested in the engine part but then we had to study like car engines as well and I don’t know why – what – where that came from. I don’t see it being relevant to my course. And we did that last year. I mean last year the course was – all the modules were really varied and we did train, buses and cars, trams, things like that. It’s not just air transport, it’s the transport industry in general, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing about the course is well we don’t have that many lectures. We don’t have that much – but the worse thing is you get a lot of course work – yeah, I think that’s one of the bad things. I mean we have 4 coming up and I haven’t actually finished – started - any of them. I’ve been really busy during Easter, I had to go and find accommodation, because I’m going on placement, for next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased that you did choose this course or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I am pleased that I did because apart from this course, I don’t know what else I’d do. So I think if it wasn’t for this course maybe I probably wouldn’t have gone to University. I know it sounds a bit extreme but I looked at all the courses and I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t want to do business, I didn’t want to do engineering, you know, sort of like mainly engineering like you know electronics or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: None?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: None.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yes. It would be nice because men they’re all – erm you know there’s nothing wrong with them – what I’m going to say is that they’re quite sort of old, I think they’re about 50, 60 you know, and they’re all male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you just have someone younger?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh it doesn’t matter. I mean they do – they’re very good at what they’re doing but it would be nice if we had like females, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. There’s no difference, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that’s good have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy having a male personal tutor or would you like to have a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t really matter, yeah, because even though he’s my personal tutor, I mean, I don’t actually see him that much (OK). But he teaches 2 of my modules and er, so I see him when I have problems with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I wouldn’t say so much the biggest influence, you know. But erm, some of the lecturers are quite good and it makes you think oh you know, I want to be – try and go into the industry because they’ve been in the industry before, and he’s worked for years and he’s been teaching now and he’ll tell you like what sort of things have happened, and how it can be fun and exciting and it can sound very interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you’ve had to do much group work as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, so far I think we’ve got – we’ve done 3 group work sort of projects.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how do you decide who you work with when you’re working in groups? Do you get put into groups or do you get to choose?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, we get put into groups.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and have you had to generally work with men or women or a mix of both?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well it’s generally men because there’s like only 10 females in my class. At the moment, I’ve got a group project and its all males. It hasn’t been a problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No? Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I think females are more hard working, I don’t know, but that’s what I feel, ‘cos men can be a bit of a – not all of them but some people in my group the men, seem a bit laid back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I’ve got one now and I had one last year. I think it’s – you know when we don’t co-operate, it didn’t – doesn’t actually work out. I didn’t actually think it’d be this hard you know like a group – because you get some members of the group who don’t want to work and they don’t turn up at meetings. I mean I’ve only seen like one person in my group, there’s 5 people and there’s 1 that never turns up and I’ve only seen him twice, you know in the whole year probably. Erm, that can be a problem and we haven’t got anything sorted out yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are benefits to doing group work though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, there are benefits, it’s just erm the work is split and you probably does less, instead of like the whole thing yourself. You get to discuss er things with other members and they can come up with great ideas as well, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the skills that you learn in group work will help you when you go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will but in the industry I think it will be a bit more hard working, yeah. I don’t think it would be how they are now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What skills do you think that you’ve learnt from the course that will help you when you’re on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well probably – probably the group work part where you have – when you have different kinds of people and you have to learn to work with them. So that’s probably one. But erm apart from that, I think it’s just what I’ve learnt in the sort of modules and what I’ve studied and just my knowledge really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel like you’re ready to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I keep thinking you know, what are they going to give me to do? And I’m really worried they might so, oh go and improve this bus network something. That I’m – yeah I’m really worried that I just might come across quite stupid, you know, I hope they won’t give me anything really hard – or I won’t understand it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you for going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think they could probably talk a bit more about the industry itself and you know, what to expect. Because at the moment I don’t really know what to expect. I mean not only in the air industry, it’s also like the transport industry, in general because we do quite a lot of other types of – kinds of transport. But a lot of people from my course have done something with air, like you know I think I’m the only person who hasn’t. They’ve all either you know, been at like an RAF camp or something, during the summer, or have flown before, you know, like as a pilot or done something to do with air, and I’m probably the only person like who hasn’t and I don’t know a lot about the industry. So, I think they could probably tell us a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you spoken to any students that have been on placement previously?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I haven’t. But – I mean we have been told a bit about you know what they do. Not a lot of people actually get placements at airports or airlines. They do logistic companies or erm you know, transport planning, that’s the main area.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know where you’re going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m going to [place].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: To the airport?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it’s like a [company].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I see why did you decide to go on placement? What attracted you to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think the main thing’s experience. I don’t have any at all, like we’ve said. Er, and the one year would be really good. It would be quite – quite a lot of experience I think. And I also think, well get away from studying for a year er because it’s quite – it’s quite hard actually where – I mean even though you get Easter and Christmas but then you work through, through those holiday periods anyway – you get so much course work and exams straight afterwards. It’s not really a holiday I don’t think, you know. I suppose that’s what I think. I want to get away for a while and earn a bit of money, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what attracted you to the company that you have got your placement with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s like a public sector company. I think maybe that what attracted me and er it’s – they’re responsible for the [____] erm in [town] and around [town] and erm I don’t think – it sounded you know, quite a good company and I wanted to apply to it because I wanted….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you apply to any other companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did. They were all transport planning based. So I mean it’s not like I didn’t want to go into airports or anything like that but there wasn’t anything available when I started applying. I mean there’s a few now like erm [name] airport but I’ve already got my placement so I didn’t apply to that one anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you look at anything like training opportunities or career prospects, anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, they didn’t actually mention a lot about you know, future prospects and things like that, but training yeah. So they sort of discussed all the – discussed in interviews that the training you along the way and quite a lot of companies now put a lot of emphasis on training. Yeah, I think with my company they do that as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how involved were the university in helping you find a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well they have a tutor who’s responsible, you know, for emailing about placements and he’s really good and you can approach him at any time. I mean I did, about my placement, because I’d been to two interviews, I failed them and then he talked me through. He talked me through them and I explained where I thought I’d gone wrong and he explained what I should have done and it does help. So he – they are quite good. I think they have – well they do have quite a lot of contacts as well and there’s quite a lot of placements coming through by email now, you know. But it’s a bit late now, when you’ve got to apply and we’ve all got placements and that’s it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything else that the university could do to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t really know. Like I said they could probably tell you what to expect and what you could be doing because erm they’ve done this for a few years now. You know, had feedback from previous placement students but we haven’t really been told much about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you’ve probably already hinted what you’re most worried about on the placement but what do you think will be the best and the worst things about being on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing will probably be having a salary – probably. And er, probably getting away from studying for a little while. Erm, the worst thing will probably be having to work 39 hours a week. Erm, and er I’m not sure about how much work you’re gonna get because I think you do get like – projects given to you. And I’ve got a brother who’s erm doing placement at the moment, and he’s studying engineering. I heard that he said he’s got a lot of projects and things like that. After you finish one you get another one. After you’ve finished another one you get another one and I’m not sure whether it’s going to be like course work, where you get like a huge load - that’s probably the only thing I’m worried about but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know yet what sort of work you will be doing on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’m not too sure, no but I just heard that I’ll be working with like other members of staff and I’ll be working in a group and that’s all I know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything you’d particularly like to do while you’re there, or wouldn’t like to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d like to learn more about the transport industry because there’s quite a lot of jobs in transport planning because the Government wants to improve the transport network and so I’ll learn as much as possible and erm I think I’ll probably go into transport planning if I enjoy the year out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll get treated differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think you do because I think you get treated as an employee, you know, because you get paid as well and er I think it’s a lot more different than er when you’re a student because there’s so many students, you know, and the lecturers can’t sort of focus on each of you individually. When you’re an employee there’s only so many, you k now, people and you get somebody who’s looking after you. That’s probably – probably quite good – what was the question, I think I’m going off the point.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, that’s fine. How do you think work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah. I can’t remember what else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, hopefully I’ll finish the course and graduate. And er, hopefully I’ll go into transport planning – if I enjoy my year out next year then I will go into transport planning, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about in say 10 years time, do you see yourself going into like managing people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think its probably something that – yeah, I’ll probably you know look forward to doing, but even if I don’t go into transport planning, you know, after I’ve graduated or something, I think I will try the air industry and I was thinking the other day, I’d probably still want to be an air stewardess, or something still in the air related industry. That’s just where my interest is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think is your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably working in the air industry. Erm, but my dream has always been like to be an air stewardess really. I think I’ll probably just do that – probably do that, you know for a few years and that’s well, what I end up doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so. Well, I will but it’s not like because it’s a male industry or anything. I mean I’d enjoy being an air hostess, there’s quite a lot of females and I’ve heard it is quite tough cos you get like er so many tests, so many rounds of you know, different kinds of tests. It will be difficult but not because er it’s a male industry…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like to work abroad then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I would like to work abroad but I’m just worried about the language difficulty. But I think, yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think the career prospects are good in air transport or transport generally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yes, because erm well the air transport industry it’s increasing and it’s you know – a lot more people – well people are travelling by air now than 10 years ago. It’s more accessible to people’s low incomes, and it is expanding and there be more planning – the same in the transport industry – the planning and all that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about once you get into the industry for like climbing the career ladder?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, God, the career ladder. I think it will be very competitive and from what I’ve heard and my experiences of trying to get into the industry, and applying for jobs – I think it will be very tough.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think I’m quite happy with – you know – what I’ve done and you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, if you had to describe the transport planning industry, erm what 5 words would you use?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, what 5 words? Erm, probably erm – transport – all the air transport or transport industry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – either or both.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well probably expanding, competitive, exciting, interesting and erm I don’t know, I can’t think of 5 things, sorry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it probably generally is but yeah, I think it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is just because of the numbers of men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yeah, because transport I think it’s always been sort of like a male thing. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think – well it’s because like back – probably about 100 years or so. Like flying was invented by men and I think it’s been controlled by men, ever since, in a way and Governments as well. That’s why probably it’s a male thing and I think males are generally more interested in planes – there’s not a lot of females around y’know that like to keep planes, or plane spotting, or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will, yeah. Like for example pilots – there are more female pilots now, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think the fact that it is male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not very much I don’t think but I don’t know yet you know until I actually graduate and apply for jobs – because the few companies that I – I’ve been to, they were more men than you know females – I could see. So it’s – maybe they’ll decide on that basis, I don’t know really, not until I’ve graduated and so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything thank you very much.
